23.0.0.en: The whole multitude of them: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders of the Jews, members of the Sanhedrin, and all their followers.

23.0.1.en: In the third trial before the council, the Jews charged Christ with claiming divinity, and sentenced Him to death according to the Jewish Law, forgetting all the prophecies that bear witness to Him. But now they brought Him to Pilate to be tried the fourth trial, and they accused Him with a charge suited to the civil authority, namely stirring up sedition, and also forbidding the payment of tribute, and then claiming that He was a king.

23.0.2.en: And of course all these were false charges, because He taught the people love and peace, and when they asked Him about the tribute He declared plainly, "Render unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's"; and as for the third charge, that He is a king, He is a spiritual king over people's hearts and never asked to be an earthly king; on the contrary, when they tried to seize Him and make Him a king, He left them and hid from their eyes, fleeing from earthly kingship (Jn 6:15). And this is the first official trial before the civil authority.

23.1.0.en: Pilate questioned Christ, as was the custom of the Romans in trying the accused, and since he noticed the simplicity of His clothing and appearance, which was not fitting for an earthly king or even merely a rich man of material standing, he asked Him, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" Christ answered, "Thou sayest it," that is, your words are true, so He confirmed his words. Pilate continued to question Christ, as St. John relates in detail in his Gospel (Jn 18:33-38), and he found no ground or charge that would warrant arresting Him, so in the end he went out to the crowds of the Jews led by the priests and scribes and declared His innocence to them.

23.2.0.en: Herod: is Herod Antipas who killed John the Baptist (Mt 14:1). When the Jews' accusations against Christ failed and His innocence appeared before the Roman authority, they stirred up the people and began to cry out, declaring that Christ was a troublemaker, in order to make Pilate doubt his judgment. And to show the gravity of the charges brought against Christ, they declared that He was a stirrer-up of the people, not only in the region of Judea, which Pilate governs, but also in Galilee, which is under the authority of another governor named Herod. Thus they put Pilate in an embarrassing position, since if he declared His innocence they would bring a charge against Christ before another governor, Herod. And in that case Pilate would be shown to be lenient toward the accused before Caesar in Rome.

23.2.1.en: So when Pilate made sure that Christ was from Galilee, and Herod, the governor of Galilee, was visiting Jerusalem, he sent Him to him to try Him so as not to exceed the authority of the governor to whom He belonged according to Roman law, and so that he could rely legally on Herod's opinion, whether for acquittal or for condemnation, in judging Christ. From this the weakness of Pilate's character appears before the pressures of the wicked Jewish leadership.

23.2.2.en: Be strong in declaring the truth however much others oppose you for their own purposes; seek God's help and His pleasure before you are swept along with those around you.

23.3.0.en: Herod had heard of Christ, His teachings and His miracles, so he longed to see Him in order to enjoy seeing His signs, and not to believe in Him or to repent of his sins; so he was glad at Pilate's sending Christ to him, and began to try Him in the fifth trial, not to know the truth but to see a miracle from Him. Christ did not answer him a word, for He knew the hardness of his heart: he had not benefited at all from the teachings of John the Baptist but killed him, and now he does not want to believe but to enjoy seeing miracles to satisfy his curiosity.

23.4.0.en: The Jews continued their pressure to prove the charges against Christ before Herod. It is the evil that reigns over the heart, however evident the truth may be.

23.5.0.en: Set him at nought: this is the second mockery of Christ, carried out by Herod and his soldiers, while the first mockery was by the temple servants and its guards in the courtyard of the high priest (ch. 22:63-65), and He was mocked a third time by the Roman soldiers in the praetorium (Mt 27:27-31; Mk 15:16-20). A gorgeous robe: which is what kings are accustomed to wear; when Herod learned that Christ claimed to be a king and saw that His clothing was lowly and not fitting for kings, then in order to carry the mockery further he put a gorgeous robe on Him. Sent him again to Pilate: Herod was not convinced by the Jews' complaint against Christ, so he did not condemn Him on any charge and sent Him back to Pilate, and by this he did not achieve the Jews' purpose.

23.5.1.en: Since Herod did not reach his aim, he expressed his anger by despising Christ, for in his eyes He was merely a weak person; and of course Christ came to call men to repentance and to lift from them the burdens of sin, and His miracles were for their relief and the strengthening of their faith.

23.5.2.en: And he did not only despise Him but mocked Him and put a soft garment of the garments of kings on Him, because he found Christ claiming to be a king while in his eyes He was a lowly person, and then he sent Him back to Pilate without finding a single charge against Him. Do you believe in Christ so that He may work miracles in your life and benefit you in your material affairs, or do you believe in Him as your Savior from every sin, so that you love Him even if you do not receive from Him your material requests?

23.6.0.en: Since Pilate respected Herod's authority and did not exceed it, the latter rejoiced and the enmity between them ended, and Satan's purpose in this was to unite the wicked against Christ; but He, amid bearing His sufferings, was seeking peace and making it, even with those who were hostile to Him.

23.6.1.en: Do you strive to make peace at all times, however much you must bear or give up?

23.7.0.en: The chief priests and scribes brought Christ back from Herod to Pilate after they had failed to support any charge against Him, and presented Christ to Pilate to be tried the sixth and last trial, whether before the Jews or the civil authority.

23.7.1.en: And after Pilate had examined Him and questioned Him, and was certain of Christ's innocence of all the charges against Him, he proposed to them that he would chastise Him, by scourging for example, to please them. Yet this is injustice, because he is confident of Christ's innocence, so why should he please the Jews and wrong Christ? All this was because of Pilate's weakness, who could not release Christ for fear of the Jews.

23.8.0.en: Pilate, as a courtesy to the Jews, used to release to them one prisoner each year, so he offered them a second proposal, which was to regard Christ as the prisoner to be released this year; but the chief priests stirred up the people and asked for the release of Barabbas, who was imprisoned for a great sedition in Jerusalem in which many were killed.

23.8.1.en: As for Christ, He is to be killed by crucifixion, that is, by the most dreadful death known at that time, so that they might be rid of Him and frighten all His followers in order to put an end to His teachings and His call.

23.9.0.en: In a heated exchange with the Jews, Pilate tried to convince the people of Christ's innocence in order to release Him, but the chief priests stirred up the people, crying out that Jesus be crucified.

23.10.0.en: Why, what evil hath he done?... I have found no cause: the third declaration by Pilate of Christ's innocence. They were instant: they repeat the crying out, demanding His crucifixion.

23.10.1.en: The voices of them prevailed: the crying grew louder and Pilate's defense weakened before it until he gave in to them.

23.10.2.en: For the third time the weak Pilate tries to release Christ because he is certain of His innocence, but the cries of the Jews increased, at the instigation of the chief priests, to pressure Pilate to crucify Christ.

23.11.0.en: Pilate finally yielded to the Jews' pressure on him since he failed to appease them, and for fear for his position he granted all their requests, released Barabbas to them and delivered Christ to them to be crucified, against his conscience, so as to remain holding to his authority and position.

23.11.1.en: If you are attached to the lusts of the world, you will not be able to declare the truth, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness; therefore repent first and strive to free yourself from your material attachments, and then you will be able to declare the truth.

23.12.0.en: They led Him outside Jerusalem to be crucified at the place of Golgotha, just as in the Old Testament the sacrifices were burned outside the camp, and they signify Christ (Heb 13:12). They laid hold upon: perhaps the first who happened to meet them, and signs of compassion for Christ's weariness and wounds may have appeared on him, so He could not continue carrying the Cross and fell under it. And because the Cross signifies shame, the Roman soldiers were not willing to carry it.

23.12.1.en: Isaiah prophesied that Christ bears the government upon His shoulders (9:6), and here He carries His Cross as the sign of His kingship, as the Psalm says that He reigned from the tree (Ps 96:10, as in the Coptic translation) (the Agpeya). And when Jesus was weary and could not continue on the way, so as not to be delayed, since they found a countryman returning from his field named Simon of Cyrene, they made him carry the Cross behind Him, because He was falling to the ground under the weight of His burden, for He had borne everything to the end. And here His perfect humanity appears, as He is also perfect God.

23.12.2.en: If Christ is the Head of the Church who reigns over it by His death on the Cross and His redemption, therefore He makes His Church share with Him in carrying the Cross through Simon the Gentile (from Cyrene in Libya), to unite to His Church the Gentiles with the Jews who believe in Him, and it is a sign for His followers that they carry His Cross behind Him, as He declared earlier to the crowds (Lk 9:23).

23.13.0.en: A great company: many of the people.

23.13.1.en: Men and women: some were of His followers, and the others were drawn by curiosity about a Jewish person being tormented who is said to be righteous.

23.13.2.en: The women showed their kind feelings in sharing Christ's sufferings by beating their breasts and lamenting, while the men rushed on, at the instigation of the priests, demanding His crucifixion. And this shows the importance of compassion and sympathy for the wronged.

23.14.0.en: Christ directed the attention of the women, indeed of the whole Jewish nation, that they should not weep for Him as a sufferer whom they love, for He suffers for the sake of all mankind to save it, and in order to receive salvation we must weep for our sins in tears of repentance, especially since our sins are what caused these sufferings to our Redeemer.

23.14.1.en: And He sees that Jerusalem will be destroyed in less than 40 years because of its lack of repentance, so He calls the women to repentance so that they might be saved from death in this destruction and find eternal life.

23.15.0.en: The days are coming: the days of the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

23.15.1.en: The barren: although the Jews count a woman who bears blessed, because she might bring forth the awaited Messiah, at the destruction of Jerusalem the flight of a pregnant woman or one carrying a child will be harder than for an ordinary woman, so the barren are called blessed. Fall on us, you mountains: either from fear of the Romans at the destruction of Jerusalem, so that they die under the mountains instead of the Romans' torturing them, or at the end of days at the coming of Christ, when they tremble and wish to flee from before His face and long for the mountains to fall on them.

23.15.2.en: Christ warns them of the destruction of Jerusalem coming upon them in AD 70, during which a severe famine would occur so that mothers would eat their children, and the barren who did not bear would be called blessed, not doing this abomination, and the Jews would flee from the Romans' violence into the mountains and caves, and wish that the mountains would fall on them instead of the torments the Romans inflicted on them.

23.15.3.en: This warning is also of the day of judgment when the glory of God appears, and the unbelievers fear and long for death to flee from Christ the Judge but cannot; and therefore Christ calls all to repentance and faith in Him that they may receive their salvation.

23.16.0.en: Christ declared that if the Jews wrong Him and kill Him, He being the green tree, that is, the green plant full of vitality, then it is to be expected that they will do more than this to the dry tree, which is the plants after they are plucked from the ground and dry up and become firewood, and it signifies men.

23.16.1.en: For fire burns the green, moist plant with difficulty, but the dry plant plucked from the ground, that is, the dry one, it burns easily. So if afflictions have come upon Christ, the green tree, it is natural that they come also upon His children, the dry tree.

23.16.2.en: Do not fear, my brother, the sufferings coming upon you, because your God supports you, so you enjoy inner peace, and this stores up glory for you in heaven.

23.17.0.en: On the way to the Cross they brought two guilty men condemned to death to be crucified with Him. Thus Christ is lifted up on the Cross as a guilty man although He is righteous and holy, since He bears our sins on His head to lift them from us.

23.18.0.en: Tradition says that the place was called the Skull because it was handed down that Adam was buried there. It is also said that this place was set apart for crucifying the guilty and was filled with the skulls of those who were killed, and therefore was called the Skull. Christ was crucified, whether in the place of Adam who fell into sin and was sentenced to death, or the place of the wicked who were killed, to die for all and save them from eternal death.

23.18.1.en: And Christ was crucified between two thieves in order to mock Him and show that He was wicked, and the Righteous One accepted that in order to die without sin and carry all our shame and our sins on His head, and by His death He buries our sins and rises to raise us in Him. Do not be troubled if they accuse you falsely, for they did so to your Lord, but trust that after your bearing of sufferings there is resurrection and glory.

23.19.0.en: Father: the sonship of Christ to God the Father appears.

23.19.1.en: Forgive them: His atoning intercession for sinners.

23.19.2.en: They know not: His seeking an excuse for sinners and His wonderful love.

23.19.3.en: They parted his raiment: they divided it into four parts, each soldier taking a part of it.

23.19.4.en: They cast lots: so as not to tear the garment which He wore, the soldiers cast lots among themselves to know who would take it. It is strange that amid severe sufferings Christ forgets Himself and is moved by love to pray for those who crucify Him, declaring His sonship to God and His perfect humanity alongside His divinity.

23.19.5.en: If only you would seek excuses for others and have compassion on sinners because they are weak, and pray for those who wrong you.

23.19.6.en: The garments of Christ point to the Church which He put on so that it became His Body, and they divided them into four parts, that is, the Church spread through the whole world with its four corners.

23.19.7.en: As for His linen coat, it was one piece woven from the top throughout, and it is said that His Virgin Mother wove it for Him. It is woven from the top, that is, heavenly, and one piece that is not torn, because His Church is one and unique, and however much the wicked try to rend it, it remains firm and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

23.20.0.en: The chosen of God: whom God chose for the redemption of the world.

23.20.1.en: The Jewish people gathered, with their religious leaders, around the Cross, rejoicing in malicious glee at the crucifixion of Christ; indeed, thinking that they had been rid of Christ and that their standing in lording it over the people had returned to them, they began to mock Him and taunt Him that He was not able to save Himself from death. But by this they themselves bore witness that Christ lived for the love and service of others and not for the comfort of Himself.

23.21.0.en: In the same sense the Roman soldiers, who were assigned to guard those crucified, mocked the crucified Christ and called on Him to save Himself if He was able, and gave Him, as was the custom of the Romans, vinegar to lessen the sense of pain, but He did not drink.

23.22.0.en: They wrote that He was the King of the Jews in the three languages well known in this place, which are Latin, which represents authority, Greek, which represents philosophy and wisdom, and Hebrew, which represents religion and the knowledge of God. All were joined together to declare that Christ is the King and Savior of His people.

23.23.0.en: It was not only the people and their leaders and also the Roman soldiers who mocked Christ, but even the wicked in the person of the thief on the left (according to tradition), who also scoffed at His weakness while hanging on the Cross, calling to Him that if He was able to save Himself, then let Him save the thieves crucified with Him.

23.23.1.en: The Evangelists Matthew and Mark mention that both thieves reviled Him, taking it that what one does, as Luke relates, is ascribed to both. So not only the crowds or the soldiers, but also the two thieves crucified with Him revile Him. Do not rush to condemn others because of how weak they appear or the consensus of opinions about it, for they may be wronged; rather say a kind word instead of condemning.

23.24.0.en: The other: the thief on the right.

23.24.1.en: Dost not thou fear God: the rebuke of the thief on the right to his fellow, because the two were near to death, so how could he rush into mockery and condemnation of another, and what would he say about this before God the Judge, whom he would meet in an hour or two, and how would he answer for all his sins.

23.24.2.en: In the same condemnation: that is, crucifixion; you ought to have sympathized with Christ because you feel how hard the sufferings of crucifixion are.

23.24.3.en: We indeed justly: the confession and repentance of the thief on the right that he was a sinner who deserved crucifixion and death.

23.24.4.en: Hath done nothing amiss: he bore witness to Christ's innocence, either from having heard of Him before, or because he saw His prayer for those who crucified Him, and also the darkness that covered the earth.

23.24.5.en: And the strange thing is that amid the frenzy of all the people against Christ and their crucifying Him, five appeared of whom it was not expected that they would bear witness to Christ's innocence and righteousness: Judas Iscariot after betraying Christ, Pilate's wife, then Pilate himself, and also the thief on the right, and finally the commander of the soldiers assigned to guard the crucified Christ. Here the virtues of the thief on the right appear) as tradition says (who forgot his sufferings and cared for the salvation of his fellow, so he rebuked him for mocking Christ, and confessed his sins and his fellow's and declared his faith in Christ's righteousness.

23.25.0.en: Then he declared his faith in the divinity of Christ, who has a heavenly kingdom, and asked Him to have mercy on him and remember him in His grace when He came into His kingdom and he left the sufferings of this perishing world.

23.25.1.en: Great is this thief's faith, greater than the disciples', who thought that Christ would reign as an earthly king. He expressed his faith with a spiritual petition, which is the salvation of the soul, not concerned with any material or spiritual request.

23.26.0.en: Christ's reply was beyond what the thief asked, for such are the mercies of God, since He granted him to share with Him in the paradise of bliss, and promised him that this would be accomplished "to day," that is, after a few hours, before the day ended. Trust that God hears you attentively in the hour of affliction and gives you more than you ask.

23.27.s.en: (6) The giving up of His spirit

23.27.0.en: Nature declared its grief at the death of its Creator for the redemption of mankind, for when mankind did not understand, inanimate creation understood, and the sun was darkened while at its brightest in the middle of the sky from the sixth hour until the ninth, that is, from twelve until three in the afternoon, and also to declare that it is because of the darkness of men's life in sin that Christ suffers and dies to save it.

23.27.1.en: As for the veil of the temple, which separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, it was rent, and the priests who were in the Holy Place saw this, and some of them believed and told of it.

23.27.2.en: It was not permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and see the ark of the covenant in it except for the high priest once a year, and now that Christ was crucified and paid the debt for us, He opened the way to the paradise of bliss and the Kingdom of Heaven, and granted us to see the temple of God in the New Testament, so that all the believers may see His temple and even partake of His most holy Body and Blood.

23.27.3.en: What exists now before the sanctuary is a curtain to show its glory and greatness, but it is opened every day so that all may enjoy the sight of God. And its presence declares the greatness and glory of the sanctuary and not its separation from the believers.

23.27.4.en: The veil of the temple was rent when Christ gave up the spirit and not before, but Luke does not care about the order of events.

23.28.0.en: Finally Christ uttered the seventh and last of His words on the Cross (three of them are mentioned in this Gospel and the rest in the other Gospels), where He puts His spirit, and indeed the spirit of mankind, into the Father's hands, because He is the firstborn among many brethren. And the devil could not hold His spirit, but Christ descended with it, united with the divinity, to hell and brought up all who believed in Him in the Old Testament, of the sons of Adam, to paradise, to wait there joyfully until the day of judgment, and then He moves them with the rest of the believers to His heavenly Kingdom. As for His body from which His spirit was separated, it remained united with His divinity. Therefore no corruption touched it in the tomb until He rose on the third day.

23.29.0.en: When the Roman centurion who was assigned to guard those crucified observed Christ during His crucifixion, and heard His words and saw what happened in nature, he believed that this man was righteous and not a criminal as the Jews claimed, and he declared his faith before all.

23.29.1.en: Take heed lest those who are far off get ahead of you in declaring their faith in God, so that they are joined to the Church and grow in their spiritual life, while you neglect your relationship with Him.

23.30.0.en: All the people: at the feast of the Passover, large numbers gather in Jerusalem, about 2 to 3 million, and many of them had heard of Jesus, so they went out to see Him being crucified.

23.30.1.en: That sight: the crucifixion of Christ.

23.30.2.en: Beheld the things which were done: the darkness that covered the earth and His words on the Cross which declare His love and righteousness, and perhaps they heard of the rending of the veil of the temple and also felt the earthquake and the rending of the rocks.

23.30.3.en: Smote their breasts: they felt that Christ was righteous and not guilty as the Jews had said, so they grieved at His death and expressed it by smiting their breasts.

23.30.4.en: Afar off: perhaps Christ's acquaintances feared the chief priests, so they stood afar off watching His crucifixion. After Christ's death on the Cross, all His loved ones and acquaintances were deeply moved, whether from Judea or those who came from Galilee as they were returning to their homes, since they felt the loss of a person very dear to them and an example of love and giving.

23.31.0.en: Joseph was from a city called Arimathaea, north of Jerusalem, and he was a counsellor, that is, one of the seventy elders, who were the leaders of the Jewish religious community, and he was distinguished by goodness and righteousness and faith in the Holy Scriptures, and he was waiting for salvation at the hands of the Messiah, and therefore he believed in Christ of whom the prophecies spoke and became His disciple, but secretly because of the pressure of the Jews and their decision to ban from Jewish worship everyone who followed Christ. And he had not consented to the persecution of Christ by the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees, whether in arresting Him or trying and crucifying Him, nor even in the attempt to catch Him in errors.

23.31.1.en: Hold fast to the truth God has revealed to you however much those around you depart from it; care for the salvation of your soul, and keep away from every evil however much others push you toward it.

23.32.0.en: Out of Joseph's love for Christ he cast off his fear, so he went to Pilate and asked him to give him the body of Jesus after He had died, to keep it with great honor, especially as he was rich and able to take care of it. Would that affliction drive you to hold fast to God and walk in His way, so that you do not fear those who obstruct you.

23.33.0.en: Pilate agreed to the request of Joseph and his colleague Nicodemus, whom the other Gospels mention, so they took the body down from the Cross and wrapped it in costly shrouds of pure linen cloth, such as the priests used to wear, for He is the High Priest who accomplished our salvation by His blood on the Cross; then they laid the body in a new tomb belonging to Joseph, in which no one had been laid before, and this was by God's arrangement, not only to honor Christ but so that when He rose from the dead no one would think that it was the body or bones of another person who had been in the tomb.

23.34.0.en: The hour was the eleventh when Christ's body was taken down and embalmed, then it was buried at the twelfth hour, and the hour of sunset drew near, when the Sabbath begins, on which the Jews must rest from all their works and not walk long distances. Some women close to Christ followed the events of His burial, such as the Virgin Mary and Mary Magdalene... and so on. These knew the place of the tomb, so they went to prepare spices and ointments and rested according to the commandment of rest on the Sabbath, and then would come with them to put them on the tomb on Sunday. This shows their love for Christ, but at the same time their not expecting His resurrection.

23.34.1.en: Chapter twenty-four: Christ's appearance to the two disciples of Emmaus and to all His disciples, and the Ascension. The events of the resurrection are mentioned in (Mt 28; Mk 16; Jn 20). The empty tomb (vv. 1-12):

23.34.2.en: 1- Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them. 2- And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. 3- And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus. 4- And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments: 5- and as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, "Why seek ye the living among the dead? 6- He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee, 7- saying, The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again." 8- And they remembered his words, 9- and returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things unto the eleven, and to all the rest. 10- It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and other women that were with them, which told these things unto the apostles.

23.34.3.en: 11- And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not. 12- Then arose Peter, and ran unto the sepulchre; and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass.
